items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I listened to Jelly Roll Morton in the back room of Steve Smith’s HRS shop at 827 Seventh Avenue when he had no place to go.

ctx.x: That was done entirely by gravity. I don’t know what formula they used to come out to – 78.26, I believe, is the standard speed – but that’s something that I could still find out about, because I have an old photograph of the man who became the head of the engineering department at Columbia Records when I went to work for them after I got out of the Army. His name is Vincent Liebler. Vin, I understand, is still alive. He must be pushing 90. This photograph shows Vin as the principal engineer in a studio at the…
I want to know what he said.

items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: like Jelly Roll Morton playing with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings on that record in 1922 I believe or ‘23

ctx.x: Well there was in the sense that in the earlier days of jazz, black musicians and white musicians tended not to play together in public. And that included phonograph records for quite a while, although as we all know from the memoirs of everybody from

Armstrong on down, after hours was a different situation. But the division even stayed on records for quite a long time, although it was broken in small ways like Jelly Roll Morton playing with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings on that record in 1922 I believe or ‘23. And that I think happened because Jelly Roll’s music was published by Melrose Brothers in Chicago, and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings also placed publications with Melrose and so it was a natural thing that Jelly Roll would participate in some of these…
